5/1/99 Editors Corner - Ethan Burrow, Prince of Austin

Well, I have a confession to make. I was crushed in the tournament in
New Orleans. I didn't get a single victory point. I was shamed... I will
explain what I did wrong so that you won't make the same mistakes when
you visit another city to play in a tournament. A special thanks to
Sorrow for showing such hospitality to TheLasombra and myself while we
visted his domain. If you care to peruse my thoughts and pictures on the
event, you can find them at my "Judgement : Camarilla Segregation -
Behind the Scenes" page.

I'd also like to take this moment to get on my soapbox and explain why I
think Misdirection should be banned in tournament play. Leaving vampires
untapped for defense is one of the many decisions methuselahs face. The
balance between offense and defense is indeed one of the basic
fundamentals of the game. I probably do not need to go into detail on
the overpoweredness of Misdirection being able to remove that element of
control from your strategy. Rather I will explain how the cost to defend
against it is so great, that the card creates an unbalance in the game
when used.

To cite example, in the recent tournament in New Orleans a dominate
weenie bleed deck used a misdirection every turn to make sure it's
prey's minions were all tapped. Every turn. If you were unfortunate
enough to have this deck be your predator, you have the following
options to avoid destruction.

1. Put as many Sudden Reversals in your deck as your predator has
Misdirections. This way you are almost guaranteed that your minions will
be unaffected. The cost to you is your master phase action every turn
for the whole game, and several card slots. Having to focus this much
resources for defense, mostly just to insure that you can *mount* a
defense, is quite unbalanced in my opinion.

2. Put 2-3 times as many Wake/untap cards in your deck as your predator
has misdirections. Even though your minions are misdirected, you can
still react or block the actions. However this method will likely take a
3rd of your deck and focus most of your decks resources against your
predator....which will not land you a victory point unless you are
playing with life boon. That's another problem entirely, but I'll table
that until it really pisses me off.

3.Play with enough Protected Resources and/or Archon Investigations to
slow down the weenie deck. And slow him down you will, but you may not
be able to completely stop them.

4.Play a weenie dominate/misdirection bleed deck and bleed your prey
faster than your predator can oust you.

I frankly don't want to see a weenie dominate/misdirection deck at every
tournament I go to for now on, but unless we ban misdirection....how
else are people going to win? Some of you may argue the rush element,
but do you really want to be the only rush deck on a table with this
thing?

Let the flame war commence <g>

Vampire of the Month -

Remilliard, Devout Crusader

He's probably the best low cost vamp you could pull into your crypt from
our clan. At a cost of 4, he's a good pick for your first minion to
influence if he shows up in your initial 4. And he's got the skills to
defend your pool while you influnce the bigger guys. And he can still be
useful later in the game.

With superior Auspex he can provide all the bleed defense and intercept
you might need in the opening turns of the game. While he has inferior
presence, he can still be used to good effect to bleed or vote with,
provided your neighbors choose to influence big vamps and thus have no
initial defense.

Take care however, for he doesn't have Celerity. He might not survive
long in combat without help.

Card of the Month -

Palla Grande

This is a nice master to place in any deck that focuses on clan Toreador
Antitrbu. The only cost is your master phase action. And for 3 turns,
all your Toreador Antitribu get +1 bleed. Whether you want to increase
bleeds for you bleed deck, or force combat with your combat decks, this
baby will do the job.

One interesting thing to note, is that it affects *all* Toreador
Antitribu. I have played games before where multiple methuselahs were
playing with Toreador Antitribu, and they all beamed when it was played
by one Methuselah. If someone in your group plays with Jost all the
time, realize that this card could benefit them as well.

How I prepared for the New Orleans tournament, and why it cost me dearly

The moment TheLasombra and I decided to make the trek to New Orleans,
one of the first things I asked were details on their Meta Game.
TheLasombra's previous encounter with them involved his Mind
Rape/Banishment deck which terrorized them to no end.

TheLasombra explained the reasons the deck performed so well : little to
no intercept and vote lock with only 2 titled vamps (no vote modifiers).
I had this in mind when I tweakedmy Vote and Bleed deck.

Without displaying the whole deck (simply because I'm lazy), it
essentially involved Jost and Rebekka for bleeds, and Natasha for
calling votes. I filled out the crypt with Arika,
Gideon, Sir Walter and Timothy, so I had titled votes and superior
presence. I bled with propoganda and social charms, and when my prey was
all tapped out I'd use domain challange. There were other toys as well,
but you get the idea. I figured this deck would take advantage of New
Orleans play style of mostly combat and give me some easy
victory points.

A day before the tournament, we got together with Sorrow and a couple of
the New Orleans players for some "friendly" games. Not only was it a lot
of fun, but it mostly confirmed everything TheLasombra had depicted of
their playing style. I deliberately did not play with my chosen
tournament deck that day. I saw no reason to show everyone how the deck
worked before round 1.

However, on tournament day I was in for quite a surprise. Sorrow had
anticipated that someone from Austin would bring a vote deck (rightly
so), and he brought his Ventrue Antitribu anti-vote deck which had
intercept and Vote denial. A new player Lauren showed up with a presence
bleed deck, which I frankly wasn't expecting either.

But the real kicker was the insideous and lame deck that Steven brought.
The ill-famed misdirection/weenie bleed template that literally sweeped
every table it was on. I was stuck on his table all but once. And on the
one game where I wasn't at his table, I had the pleasure of contesting
Sir Walter with my prey Norm. No victory points for me.

What did I learn ?

Meta Games are predictable except for tournaments. Everyone goes in with
a different mindset than under normal gaming days.

Expect and plan for the worst of decks, not the decks you've seen your
opponents play. I was wrong to assume that I was going to face only
combat heavy decks.

Speed is paramount in tournaments, not staying power. Pool gaining
resources and large capacity vamps may seem like good ideas....but will
it come out in time to defend yourself against the weenie horde? And
rest assured, there will always be one weenie horde in each
tournament...or that city is doing it wrong.

Deck Medic/Strategy Corner

The one gleaming gem from the New Orleans experience, is TheLasombra's
Aggressive Tactics deck which took 6 victory points and made it to the
finals. This deck using the Toreador Antitribu is pretty nasty, and I

Ethan wrote:
>>I'd also like to take this moment to get on my soapbox and explain why I
think Misdirection should be banned in tournament play. Leaving vampires
untapped for defense is one of the many decisions methuselahs face. The
balance between offense and defense is indeed one of the basic
fundamentals of the game. I probably do not need to go into detail on
the overpoweredness of Misdirection being able to remove that element of
control from your strategy. Rather I will explain how the cost to defend
against it is so great, that the card creates an unbalance in the game
when used.>>

I really don't think Misdirection is all that powerful. When building a deck,
you need to take into account how you are going to defend yourself. If your
main defense is blocking, you need to be able to deal with stealth and be able
to untap reliably, otherwise your blocking defense simply isn't going to be
effective. If the only defense of your deck is leaving vampires untapped and
hoping they don't have blasters..er..I mean stealth, you probably aren't going
to survive very long, Misdirection or no. An intercept deck (or any deck that
relies on blocking reliably) is going to need a good supply of intercept and
untaps to work, and thus doesn't need to worry about Misdirection all that
much. Just standing around and hoping to block an opponent gets you
nowhere--what if they have stealth? What if they have Misdirection? In both
cases, you end up dead. Thus, you need to take these things into account, and
generally not rely on standing around to block, hoping your opponent doesn't
have Misdirection.

>>To cite example, in the recent tournament in New Orleans a dominate
weenie bleed deck used a misdirection every turn to make sure it's
prey's minions were all tapped. Every turn. If you were unfortunate
enough to have this deck be your predator, you have the following
options to avoid destruction.>>

If his prey's vampires were all tapped out every turn doing things that were
useful, instead of standing around hoping that the Dominate deck didn't have a
Misdirection, A) they would have done much better and B) the Dominate deck
would have a whole deck full of useless Master cards.

>>1. Put as many Sudden Reversals in your deck as your predator has
Misdirections.

2. Put 2-3 times as many Wake/untap cards in your deck as your predator
has misdirections.

3.Play with enough Protected Resources and/or Archon Investigations to

slow down the weenie deck.

4.Play a weenie dominate/misdirection bleed deck and bleed your prey

faster than your predator can oust you.

I frankly don't want to see a weenie dominate/misdirection deck at every
tournament I go to for now on, but unless we ban misdirection....how
else are people going to win? Some of you may argue the rush element,
but do you really want to be the only rush deck on a table with this
thing?>>

Or, play a deck that can deal with such a speedy deck and doesn't rely on
standing around and trying to block. The basic defense strategies one can use
against Bleeding are:

A) Block: To be good at this, you need to have reliable intercept and reliable
untaps. Without both, the Block strategy simply won't be effective.

B) Race: Be just as fast, or faster, than your predator. In this situation your
vampires are always tapped out and the existance of Misdirection has no effect
on the deck.

C) Bounce: Like the Block defense, the Bounce defense needs reliable untap to
work with the Bounce, otherwise it just won't work, Misdirection or no.

D) Pool Gain: Gain an awful lot of pool really fast. You won't care that your
predator is bleeding you.

E) Rush: Kill their vampires. They can't bleed you. Your vampires are tapped
out every turn, so again, the Misdirection has no bearing on the game.

Of these basic defense strategies, Block and Bounce are affected by
Misdirection, but only if you don't have reliable untap, and if you don't,
again, your deck isn't going to have particular success vs any sort of bleed
deck.

Misdirection is incredibly handy in environments where everyone plans on
blocking out of sheer habit. In environments where decks only plan on blocking
when they are designed to block stuff, the Misdirection becomes much less
useful.

I'd be perfectly happy to be at a table as the only Rush deck with said weenie
Dominate deck (i'd be even happier if I was the second Rush deck at the table
:-). Rush decks can be just as fast, the weenie Dominate deck generally has
zero combat defense, and their little vampires are never coming out of torpor.
He gets out a vampire, I torporize it. He gets out two, I torporize two. And so
on.

Yes, weenie bleed decks are very powerful, probably overly so (but that is due
to the game design as a whole, not because of Misdirection), but you can build
decks that are perfectly competetive and also able to compete with such decks.
You need to accept the fact that you might be the prey of a deck that can
Misdirect you every turn, realize that it is going tobe very good at killing
you, and build a deck that can deal with it. And it can be done without tons of
SR, AI, or PR, using basic strategies.

In many tournaments, you'll find that if your grandpredator is weak

vampires and allow the predator to mount some small defense (or, if
he chooses, some small offense).

*) It is not supported by any incarnation of the rulebook.
*) The game's designer said that it wasn't supposed to work that way.
*) It detracts from the game by increasing the King-maker effect.

to Misdirection.

Sometimes you just get killed. Had he been bleeding you with stealth instead of
Misdirection, it is just as likely that you would have been bled for just as
much just as quickly. How much intercept were you packing? If you were packing
enough to stop a reliable S+B deck, and were relying on it as your main
defense, you probably should have had more untaps. Sometimes, however, even in
the best situations, your cards don't fall right, and then you are just killed.
It happens.

>>With one played every single turn by the Methuselah playing them, you die.>>

Unless you don't care wheither or not you are untapped.

>>B is Wrong. Remember you can pay 0 for cards that have X as their cost
every turn to cycle your hand, and since you were planning on playing
it anyway, you simply saved some pool. Therefore, you have no useless master
cards in hand when you are ready to bleed.>>

Notice I said "useless" and not "unplayable". You can still cycle the
Misdirections, they just don't do you any good.

>>How do you define things that are useful? Every turn that other decks
were its prey they tried to oust their own prey. In this particular case
it didn't work. The only thing that would have saved them was the inclusion
of Rush, which sadly did not make an appearance at that tournament.>>

Ahh. If only more people had the strength of will to play Rush decks :-)

That is why Rush decks need to exist--they are the Rock to this sort of deck's
Scisors, and if no one is playing Rock, Scisors wins a lot more often than it
should. However, I also don't believe that Rush was the only thing that would
have stopped it. Another deck just as fast would have killed it--what was its
predator doing while it was tapping out every turn killing you? If its predator
had been fast as well, the weenie dominate deck would have been smashed. A more
reliable Intercept deck would have stopped it as well.

>>Agreed. 8 Forced Awakenings plus bringing out a vampire every turn
is usually considered reliable. It was not.>>

Sometimes your deck just doesn't work. That, and a dedicated intercept defense
really needs more than 8 untaps in 90 cards. That is one of the failings of the
intercept defense--it takes up way too much of your deck space to be reliable.
The intercept deck I posted in my latest Nosferatu Newsletter has 23 untap
cards (5 FA, 5 Rats, 6 2nd, 7 Cats), and it still often isn't enough.

I think your perception here may be incorrect. Weenie hordes do
tend to dominate tournaments (whether or not they use Dominate ;-)
in my view.

Take the Los Angeles tournament scene - probably the biggest one
in the country, from what I've heard. Weenie dominate bleed decks
(with Misdirection?) have been all over their tourneys for quite some
time. I'm not sure that they always win, but they are certainly a
well-known force. Weenie presence bleed won one of the Ithaca tourneys
I ran (Steve Wampler's deck). Rush decks are typically at least semi-
weenie decks; a rush deck with an average capacity over 4 is probably
too slow to be competitive in a tourney environment. Weenie vote is
one of the enduring archetypes as well.

Weenie decks *are* inherently more efficient than non-weenie decks
because they pay less pool to get the same number of actions as
everyone else, or the same amount of pool to get more actions. And
actions are one of the key resources in Jyhad, as I think everyone
knows? (First you get the actions, then you get the power, then you get
the women...)

If you Misdirect someone's minions, you have essentially robbed them
of their actions by paying pool. This is good because it means
the person you Misdirect gets less use out of his/her minions than
you do out of yours. It is useful, then, in the same way that playing
a Wake is useful: it gains an 'action equivalent' when you play it.
Note that Wake costs a card but no pool to play; however, Misdirection
can produce more than a one-'action equivalent' swing. Although the
pool cost adheres to the 'offense is more expensive than defense'
principle, the multi-minion factor may make Misdirection somewhat
overpowered.

Still, I'm skeptical that Misdirection is really banning material. To
me it looks like being on the high end of the remaining powerful-masters
range: it is about as nasty as Anarch Revolt, Society of Leopold, Hostile
Takeover; somewhat nastier than Curse of Nitocris or Minion Tap; much
nastier than Metro Underground or Deal with the Devil.

As Peter has said, the most effective way to deal with Misdirection is
to be able to ignore it, by building a deck that expects to tap out
its minions every turn. If you are not doing this, you are effectively
robbing yourself of actions if you do not block successfully. Misdirection
may cause you to lose those actions, but so would Mind Numb, Pentex
Subversion, excessive stealth, Banishment, or a successful Bum's Rush on
the untapped vampire.

game environment, then the card needs to be looked at.

overpowered for it's cost. While other playgroups may not be as
affected by Misdirection than Austin's or New Orlean's, I still think
